{{short description|Mathematical equation}}
In [[isotropic]] [[turbulence]] the '''Kármán–Howarth''' equation (after [[Theodore von Kármán]] and [[Leslie Howarth]] 1938), which is derived from the [[Navier–Stokes equations]], is used to describe the evolution of non-dimensional longitudinal [[autocorrelation]].<ref>De Karman, T., & Howarth, L. (1938). On the statistical theory of isotropic turbulence. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 164(917), 192–215.</ref><ref>Monin, A. S., & Yaglom, A. M. (2013). Statistical fluid mechanics, volume II: Mechanics of turbulence (Vol. 2). Courier Corporation.</ref><ref>Batchelor, G. K. (1953). The theory of homogeneous turbulence. Cambridge university press.</ref><ref>Panchev, S. (2016). Random Functions and Turbulence: International Series of Monographs in Natural Philosophy (Vol. 32). Elsevier.</ref><ref>Hinze, J. O. (1959). Turbulence, (1975). New York.</ref>

==Mathematical description==
Consider a two-point velocity correlation tensor for homogeneous turbulence

: <math>R_{ij}(\mathbf{r},t) = \overline{u_i(\mathbf{x},t) u_j(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{r},t)}.</math>

For isotropic turbulence, this correlation tensor can be expressed in terms of two scalar functions, using the [[invariant theory]] of full rotation group, first derived by [[Howard P. Robertson]] in 1940,<ref>Robertson, H. P. (1940, April). The invariant theory of isotropic turbulence. In Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society (Vol. 36, No. 2, pp. 209–223). Cambridge University Press.</ref>

:<math>R_{ij}(\mathbf{r},t) = u'^2 \left\{ [f(r,t)-g(r,t)]\frac{r_ir_j}{r^2} + g(r,t) \delta_{ij}\right\}, \quad f(r,t) = \frac{R_{11}}{u'^2}, \quad g(r,t) = \frac{R_{22}}{u'^2}</math>

where <math>u'</math> is the [[root mean square]] turbulent velocity and <math>u_1,\ u_2, \ u_3</math> are turbulent velocity in all three directions. Here, <math>f(r)</math> is the longitudinal correlation and <math>g(r)</math> is the lateral correlation of velocity at two different points. From continuity equation, we have

:<math>\frac{\partial R_{ij}}{\partial r_j}=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad g(r,t) = f(r,t) + \frac{r}{2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r}f(r,t)</math>

Thus <math>f(r,t)</math> uniquely determines the two-point correlation function. [[Theodore von Kármán]] and [[Leslie Howarth]] derived the evolution equation for <math>f(r,t)</math> from [[Navier–Stokes equation]] as

:<math>\frac \partial {\partial t} (u'^2 f) - \frac{u'^3}{r^4} \frac \partial {\partial r} (r^4 h) = \frac{2\nu u'^2}{r^4} \frac\partial {\partial r} \left(r^4 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right)</math>

where <math>h(r,t)</math> uniquely determines the triple correlation tensor

: <math>S_{ij} = {} \frac{\partial }{\partial r_k} \left( \overline{u_i(\mathbf{x},t) u_k(\mathbf{x},t)u_j(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{r},t)}-\overline{u_i(\mathbf{x},t) u_k(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{r},t)u_j(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{r},t)}\right).</math>

==Loitsianskii's invariant==

L.G. Loitsianskii derived an integral invariant for the decay of the turbulence by taking the fourth moment of the Kármán–Howarth equation in 1939,<ref>Loitsianskii, L. G. (1939) Einige Grundgesetze einer isotropen turbulenten Strömung. Arbeiten d. Zentr. Aero-Hydrdyn. Inst., 440.</ref><ref>Landau, L. D., & Lifshitz, E. M. (1959). Fluid Mechanics Pergamon. New York, 61.</ref> i.e.,

:<math>\frac \partial {\partial t} \left(u'^2 \int_0^\infty r^4 f\ dr\right) = \left[2\nu u'^2 r^4 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} + u'^3 r^4 h\right]_0^\infty.</math>

If <math>f(r)</math> decays faster than <math>r^{-3}</math> as <math>r\rightarrow\infty</math> and also in this limit, if we assume that <math>r^4 h</math> vanishes, we have the quantity,

:<math>\Lambda = u'^2 \int_0^\infty r^4 f\ dr = \mathrm{constant}</math>

which is invariant. [[Lev Landau]] and [[Evgeny Lifshitz]] showed that this invariant is equivalent to [[conservation of angular momentum]].<ref>Landau, L. D., & Lifshitz, E. M. (1987). Fluid mechanics. 1987. Course of Theoretical Physics.</ref> However, Ian Proudman and W.H. Reid showed that this invariant does not hold always since <math>\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty} (r^4 h)</math> is not in general zero, at least, in the initial period of the decay.<ref>Proudman, I., & Reid, W. H. (1954). On the decay of a normally distributed and homogeneous turbulent velocity field. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A, 247(926), 163-189.</ref><ref>Batchelor, G. K., & Proudman, I. (1956) The large-scale structure of homogeneous turbulence. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A, 248(949), 369-405.</ref> In 1967, [[Philip Saffman]] showed that this integral depends on the initial conditions and the integral can diverge under certain conditions.<ref>Saffman, P. G. (1967). The large-scale structure of homogeneous turbulence. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 27(3), 581-593.</ref>

==Decay of turbulence==
For the viscosity dominated flows, during the decay of turbulence, the Kármán–Howarth equation reduces to a [[heat equation]] once the triple correlation tensor is neglected, i.e.,

:<math>\frac \partial {\partial t} (u'^2 f)  = \frac{2\nu u'^2}{r^4} \frac\partial {\partial r} \left(r^4 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right).</math>

With suitable boundary conditions, the solution to above equation is given by<ref>Spiegel, E. A. (Ed.). (2010). The Theory of Turbulence: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's 1954 Lectures (Vol. 810). Springer.</ref>

:<math>f(r,t) =  e^{-r^2/8\nu t}, \quad u'^2 = \mathrm{const.}\times (\nu t)^{-5/2}</math>

so that,

:<math>R_{ij}(r,t) \sim (\nu t)^{-5/2} e^{-r^2/8\nu t}.</math>
